definition: The smallest unit of sound in a language that distinguishes one word from another. Phonemes are abstract mental representations; their physical realizations are allophones.
A phonetic variant of a phoneme that does not change meaning. Allophones occur in predictable phonetic environments defined by phonological rules.
Two words that differ by only a single phoneme in the same position, used to demonstrate that two sounds are distinct phonemes in a language.
A formal statement describing how phonemes are systematically altered in certain phonetic environments. Written as A → B / C _ D, meaning A becomes B when preceded by C and followed by D.
A phonological process in which a sound becomes more similar to a neighboring sound in terms of place or manner of articulation. Can be regressive (anticipatory) or progressive.
A phonological process in which a sound becomes less similar to a neighboring sound, often to make the two sounds easier to distinguish.
A phonological process in which all vowels within a word must share a common feature (e.g., front/back or ATR). Common in Turkic and Mongolian languages.
A process by which a nasal consonant takes on the place of articulation of a following stop consonant.
A weakening of consonants, often as a result of being in a medial or intervocalic position. Examples include voicing of stops and spirantization.
The change of a stop consonant into a fricative or spirant, a common type of lenition.
A phonological process in which two sounds switch positions within a word.
The insertion of a sound (usually a vowel) into a word, often to break up an otherwise impermissible consonant cluster.
The deletion of a vowel, typically an unstressed one, from within a word (not at the beginning or end).
The loss of a sound or sounds at the end of a word.
The constraints on permissible sound sequences in a language. Phonotactic rules specify which sounds may appear in which positions (onset, nucleus, coda) and what clusters are allowed.
The internal organization of a syllable into onset, nucleus, and coda. Commonly represented as (C)V(C) or through moraic theory.
The consonant or consonant cluster that begins a syllable, preceding the nucleus.
The consonant or consonant cluster that follows the nucleus of a syllable.
The core of a syllable, typically a vowel or syllabic consonant. The nucleus is the only obligatory part of a syllable.
A unit of syllabic weight. Short vowels are monomoraic; long vowels and diphthongs are bimoraic. Used in quantity-sensitive phonological processes.
The relative prominence of a syllable, typically realized through greater loudness, pitch, or duration. Languages vary in whether stress is fixed, free, or predictable.
The use of pitch to distinguish lexical or grammatical meaning. Tonal languages include Mandarin, Yoruba, and many Southeast Asian languages.
A system in which pitch is used to distinguish words but each word has only one accented syllable rather than multiple tones.
The location in the vocal tract where airflow is most constricted during the production of a consonant. Includes bilabial, labiodental, dental, alveolar, palatal, velar, and uvular.
The way airflow is modified in producing a consonant: stop, fricative, affricate, nasal, approximant, trill, tap, etc.
The vibration of the vocal folds during the production of a sound. Voiced sounds (e.g. /b/, /d/) involve vibration; voiceless sounds (e.g. /p/, /t/) do not.
Two sounds are in complementary distribution when they never appear in the same phonetic environment. This is evidence that they are allophones of the same phoneme.
Two sounds are in free variation when they can substitute for each other without changing word meaning and without being conditioned by phonetic environment.

Advanced Tongue Root — a phonological feature distinguishing vowels produced with the tongue root pushed forward (+ATR) from those with it retracted (-ATR). Significant in vowel harmony systems of West African and East African languages.
A sequence of two or more consonants without an intervening vowel. Languages vary in which clusters are permitted by their phonotactics.
The smallest meaningful unit in a language. Morphemes can be free (can stand alone as a word) or bound (must attach to another morpheme).
A morpheme that can stand alone as a word (e.g., 'book', 'run', 'happy').
A morpheme that cannot stand alone and must attach to another morpheme. Includes prefixes, suffixes, infixes, and circumfixes.
A bound morpheme attached to a base or stem to derive a new form or mark grammatical categories. Types include prefix, suffix, infix, circumfix, suprafix, and transfix.
An affix attached to the beginning of a base or stem.
An affix attached to the end of a base or stem.
An affix inserted within the base of a word rather than at its edges. Common in Tagalog and some Native American languages.
An affix consisting of two parts that attach to both ends of a base simultaneously. Also called a discontinuous affix.
A phonological variant of a morpheme. For example, the English plural morpheme has allomorphs /-s/, /-z/, and /-ɪz/ depending on the final sound of the base.
The core morpheme of a word that carries its basic lexical meaning, to which affixes may be added. Distinct from stem, which may include some affixes.
The form of a word to which inflectional affixes are attached. A stem may be identical to the root or may include derivational affixes.
The form to which any morphological operation applies. A base is more general than root or stem, as it can be a simple root, a derived form, or even a compound.

The process of adding morphological material to a word to mark grammatical categories such as tense, aspect, number, case, gender, or agreement, without changing the word's core meaning or part of speech.
The process of forming a new word from an existing one, typically changing its meaning or part of speech (e.g., 'happy' → 'happiness').
The complete set of inflected forms of a word. For example, the paradigm of a Latin noun includes all case and number forms.
The inflection of nouns, pronouns, and adjectives for case, number, and gender. Languages that organize nouns into classes with similar paradigms are said to have declension classes.
The inflection of verbs for categories such as tense, aspect, mood, voice, person, and number.
A systematic vowel alternation within a root that signals grammatical distinctions. The English strong verb system shows ablaut: sing/sang/sung.
A type of vowel alternation in which a vowel is fronted due to a front vowel or /j/ in a following syllable. The German plural umlaut (Fuß → Füße) is a well-known example.
Any systematic alternation of sounds within a morpheme to signal a grammatical or lexical contrast. Includes ablaut and umlaut as subtypes.
An inflectional relationship between two forms of the same lexeme where the forms share no phonological resemblance (e.g., English 'go'/'went', 'good'/'better').
A morphological process that copies all or part of a base to signal a grammatical or lexical meaning, such as plurality, intensity, or repetition.

A morphological type in which words are formed by stringing together morphemes that are clearly separable and each corresponds to a single grammatical meaning. Finnish and Swahili are classic examples.
A morphological type (also called inflecting or synthetic) in which a single morpheme expresses multiple grammatical meanings simultaneously. Latin case endings are a typical example.
A morphological type in which words consist of single morphemes with no inflection. Grammatical relations are expressed through word order and particles. Mandarin is a prototypical example.
A morphological type in which words contain many morphemes and can express what other languages might say in an entire sentence. Common in indigenous North American languages.
The classification of languages according to their dominant morphological strategy: isolating, agglutinative, fusional, or polysynthetic. Most languages exhibit features of more than one type.
A process in which a nominal (noun) is incorporated into a verb to form a compound predicate. Particularly common in polysynthetic languages.
A word formed by combining two or more free morphemes or roots. Compounds may be endocentric (the meaning is a hyponym of one constituent) or exocentric.
The set of morphological and phonological processes used to create new words, including derivation, compounding, reduplication, and conversion.
An invisible or phonologically null morpheme that nonetheless carries grammatical meaning, as in English 'sheep' (plural unmarked) or 'cut' (past tense unmarked).
A morpheme that behaves phonologically like an affix (attached to a host) but syntactically like an independent word. English 's (possessive) and 'll (future) are clitics.
The hierarchical organization of words into phrases and clauses. Phrase structure rules specify how constituents are combined; commonly represented in tree diagrams.
A syntactic unit that functions as part of a larger construction. Constituents are identified by constituency tests such as substitution, movement, and coordination.
The obligatory, central element of a phrase that determines the phrase's category and distributional properties. Phrases are named after their heads: NP, VP, AP, PP.
A syntactic argument that completes the meaning of the head. The complement is typically selected (subcategorized) by the head.
An optional syntactic constituent that modifies a head or phrase without being selected by it. Adjuncts are typically adverbs, adverbials, or prepositional phrases.
In X-bar theory, the position at the edge of a maximal projection that is occupied by determiners, degree modifiers, or subjects.
A theory of phrase structure in which every phrase has an intermediate bar-level (X') between the head (X) and the maximal projection (XP), allowing for a uniform hierarchical template.
The canonical order of subject, verb, and object in declarative clauses. Common typological patterns are SOV, SVO, VSO, VOS, OVS, and OVS.
Subject-Object-Verb word order. The most common order cross-linguistically, found in Japanese, Turkish, and Hindi.
Subject-Verb-Object word order. Characteristic of English, French, Mandarin, and Swahili.
Verb-Subject-Object word order. Common in Classical Arabic, Welsh, and many Austronesian languages.
A grammatical relationship in which one word (the controller) determines the morphological form of another word (the target). Common agreement features include person, number, gender, and case.
The specification of the number and type of arguments (subject, object, indirect object) that a predicate requires. Closely related to the verb's semantic role assignment.
The number of arguments a predicate takes. Intransitive verbs have valency 1; transitive verbs have valency 2; ditransitive verbs have valency 3.
The property of a verb that determines whether it takes a direct object. Transitive verbs require an object; intransitive verbs do not.
A subordinate clause that modifies a noun (the head noun) and is typically introduced by a relative pronoun. Relative clauses are classified as prenominal, postnominal, or internally headed.
The syntactic relationship in which one clause (the subordinate) is embedded within another (the main clause).
The joining of two or more clauses or phrases of equal syntactic status using a coordinating conjunction (and, or, but).

A grammatical category that marks the syntactic role of a noun phrase (subject, object, indirect object, possessor, etc.). Realized morphologically (through declension) or syntactically (through position).
The case assigned to the subject of a clause in nominative-accusative alignment systems.
The case assigned to the direct object of a verb in nominative-accusative alignment systems.
The case assigned to the indirect object or recipient argument in many languages, also used for beneficiaries and goals.
The case that typically marks possessors or associates. Also used to express partitivity and measure in many languages.
A grammatical category that locates an event in time, typically relative to the moment of speech (present, past, future) or to another reference point.
A grammatical category that expresses the internal temporal structure of an event: whether it is complete (perfective), ongoing (imperfective), habitual, etc.
A grammatical category that expresses the speaker's attitude toward the proposition: indicative (factual), subjunctive (hypothetical), imperative (command), conditional, etc.
A grammatical category relating to the relationship between the verb and its arguments, particularly which argument is the syntactic subject. Includes active, passive, and middle voice.
A voice construction in which the patient or theme argument is promoted to subject position and the agent is demoted or omitted.
The underlying thematic relationship between a noun phrase and the predicate (verb). Core semantic roles include agent, patient, theme, experiencer, recipient, goal, and source.
A formal label for the semantic relationship between a predicate and its arguments. The theta-criterion holds that each argument receives exactly one theta role.
The semantic role assigned to the willful initiator or performer of an action.
The semantic role assigned to the entity that is affected by or undergoes the action or change described by the verb.
The semantic role assigned to the entity that perceives or has an internal experience described by a psychological predicate (e.g., 'John knows the answer').
The study of word meaning, including sense relations (synonymy, antonymy, hyponymy), componential analysis, prototype theory, and lexical fields.
The meaning of a linguistic expression defined by its relationship to other expressions in the language system, as opposed to reference (the real-world entity it denotes).
The real-world entity or set of entities that a linguistic expression picks out in a given context.
The literal or primary meaning of a word, as opposed to its connotations. The denotation of 'dog' is any member of the species Canis lupus familiaris.
The secondary, associative, or evaluative meanings that a word carries beyond its literal denotation.
The relationship between two words that have the same or very similar meaning. True (full) synonymy is rare; most synonyms differ in register, connotation, or collocations.
The sense relation of opposite meaning. Includes gradable antonyms (hot/cold), complementary antonyms (alive/dead), and relational antonyms (buy/sell).
The sense relation in which one word (the hyponym) is more specific than another (the hyperonym or superordinate). 'Dog' is a hyponym of 'animal'.
The property of a single word having multiple related senses (e.g., 'bank' as a financial institution and as the side of a river — though these may be homonyms rather than polysemes).
The relationship between two words that share the same form but have unrelated meanings (e.g., 'bat' the animal vs. 'bat' the implement).
The principle that the meaning of a complex expression is a function of the meanings of its parts and the syntactic rules combining them.

The phenomenon of expressions whose interpretation depends on contextual features such as the speaker, hearer, time, or place. Includes personal (I/you), temporal (now/then), and spatial (here/there) deixis.
The semantic domain covering necessity, possibility, permission, and obligation. Grammatically expressed through modal verbs, moods, or particles.
Modality relating to the speaker's degree of certainty about a proposition (certainty, probability, possibility).
Modality relating to obligation, permission, or prohibition. Deontic must means 'it is required that'; deontic may means 'it is permitted that'.

Lexical aspect or situation type — the inherent temporal structure of a verb or predicate independent of grammatical aspect. Includes states, activities, accomplishments, and achievements (Vendler classes).
A semantic property of predicates that have a natural endpoint. Telic predicates describe events with an inherent culmination; atelic predicates do not.

The case (or alignment) assigned to the agent of a transitive verb in ergative-absolutive systems. Contrasts with absolutive, which marks both the patient of transitive verbs and the single argument of intransitive verbs.
The case that marks the single argument of an intransitive predicate and the patient of a transitive predicate in an ergative-absolutive alignment system.

An alignment system in which the subject of both transitive and intransitive verbs is treated the same (nominative), while the object of a transitive verb receives a different case (accusative). The most common alignment cross-linguistically.
A system in which a language uses ergative-absolutive alignment in some contexts and nominative-accusative alignment in others, often conditioned by tense, aspect, or person.

The grammatical pattern that determines how the S (subject of intransitive), A (agent of transitive), and P (patient of transitive) arguments are marked. Major types are nominative-accusative and ergative-absolutive.
A cross-linguistically varying grammatical feature that can take a small number of values and tends to correlate with other typological properties.
A typological property in which grammatical information about arguments is marked on the head of a phrase (e.g., agreement on the verb) rather than on the dependents.
A typological property in which grammatical information is marked on the dependent of a construction rather than on the head. Case marking on nouns is an example.
A typological property of languages that allow the subject (or object) pronoun to be omitted when recoverable from context or verb agreement. Spanish and Italian are pro-drop; English is not.
A morpheme used with numerals to categorize the noun it quantifies according to semantic properties (animacy, shape, size). Common in Mandarin, Japanese, and Burmese.

A grammatical categorization of nouns into classes based on semantic or formal properties. Classes often trigger agreement on adjectives, verbs, and determiners. Bantu languages have elaborate noun class systems.
A system for classifying nouns into groups (genders) that trigger agreement on other words. Genders may correlate with biological sex (masculine/feminine) or be semantically arbitrary.

A grammatical category that obligatorily encodes the source of the speaker's information about an event: direct witness, reported speech, inference, etc. Grammaticalized in Quechua, Tibetan, and many other languages.
A grammatical category encoding whether information is new or unexpected to the speaker. Grammaticalized in some languages alongside evidentiality.

A semantic property that classifies referents on a scale from most animate (humans, animals) to least animate (abstract concepts, inanimate objects). Animacy hierarchies affect agreement, case, and word order in many languages.
A grammatical category used in Algonquian languages that distinguishes between a proximate third person (the more salient referent) and an obviative third person (the less salient referent).
A tonal system in which each syllable is assigned a tone on a discrete scale (high, mid, low) without complex contour distinctions. Contrasts with contour tone systems.

A Semitic morphological pattern in which a root consisting of three consonants (a triliteral skeleton) carries core lexical meaning, while vowel patterns and affixes mark derivational and inflectional categories.
Morphological processes in which morphemes are not simply strung end-to-end but interdigitated or overlaid with the base (transfixes, templates). Characteristic of Semitic languages.
A morphological system in which words are formed by mapping a root onto an abstract canonical pattern (template) that specifies the distribution of vowels and consonants.
Morphological processes in which morphemes are combined by simple linear concatenation (affixation, compounding). Contrasts with nonconcatenative morphology.
A verb (typically 'be') that links a subject to a predicate nominal or predicate adjective. Some languages lack a copula in present-tense equative sentences (null copula).
The element of a sentence (typically a verb phrase) that says something about the subject. In formal semantics, a predicate denotes a property or relation.
A closed-class word that specifies the reference of a noun phrase (definite article, indefinite article, demonstrative, quantifier).
A functional element that introduces a subordinate clause, marking it as a complement. In English, 'that' in 'I know that he left' is a complementizer.
A construction in which the subject of a sentence is phonologically absent but interpretable from context or verb agreement. See pro-drop.
The domain over which an operator (quantifier, negation, modal) takes effect. Scope relations determine the truth conditions of complex sentences.
An expression that specifies the quantity of a noun phrase: universal (every, all), existential (some, a), cardinal (three), etc.
The semantic operation of reversing the truth value of a proposition. Morphosyntactically realized as negative particles, affixes, or polarity verbs.
The distinction between positive (affirmative) and negative constructions. Polarity items (e.g., 'any', 'ever') are sensitive to the polarity environment.
Phonological changes that occur at morpheme or word boundaries due to the influence of neighboring sounds. Includes vowel sandhi, tone sandhi, and consonant sandhi.
In French, the pronunciation of a normally silent word-final consonant before a following word beginning with a vowel. A type of external sandhi.
The omission of a sound or syllable in connected speech, often at word boundaries.
A phonological process in which a consonant is strengthened, e.g., a fricative becoming a stop. The opposite of lenition.
The assignment of segments to syllables. Languages follow the maximal onset principle (prefer larger onsets) subject to phonotactic constraints.
The relative heaviness of a syllable, determined by the number of moras. Heavy syllables (two moras) differ from light syllables (one mora) in stress assignment and prosodic patterns.
A metrical unit that groups syllables into a rhythmic unit. Common foot types include the iamb (light-heavy), trochee (heavy-light), and dactyl.
A resemblance relationship between the form of a sign and its meaning. Sound symbolism (phonesthesia) and onomatopoeia are examples of iconic motivation in language.
The property of language whereby the relationship between a linguistic form and its meaning is conventional and unmotivated. Contrasted with iconicity.
Words whose phonological form imitates or resembles the sound they denote (e.g., 'buzz', 'meow', 'splash').
A non-arbitrary relationship between sound and meaning, where certain sounds or sound patterns are associated with particular semantic properties cross-linguistically.
A class of expressions that share distributional and morphosyntactic properties. Includes parts of speech (noun, verb, adjective) and inflectional categories (tense, case, number).
A major syntactic-semantic category of words such as noun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition/postposition, conjunction, determiner, and pronoun.
A morpheme that classifies the noun it modifies according to semantic features like shape, animacy, or function. Distinct from noun class systems but related.
A case or grammatical relation marking location. Some languages grammaticalize a rich set of locative distinctions (interior, surface, proximity).
A case that marks the instrument or means by which an action is performed.
A case used to address someone directly. In many languages, the vocative is formally distinct from the nominative.
The element of a sentence that names what the sentence is about; often sentence-initial. Topic differs from subject in being a discourse category rather than a purely grammatical one.
The element of a sentence that presents new or contrastive information. Marked through prosody (stress), morphology, or syntactic movement in different languages.
The way a sentence packages given (old) vs. new information for the discourse participant. Includes topic-comment and focus-background articulations.
